Chapter 9. Conventional Wisdom: Why the Obvious Answer Is Often Wrong.
Let’s be honest—there’s a certain comfort in thinking the world is simple, that the answers are right in front of us, and experts always have it figured out.
But, as you’ve probably noticed by now, life rarely works that way. In fact, some of the biggest surprises come when what seems obvious just isn’t true—and the real story? It’s usually much more interesting.
Think about the fear of strangers—the kind that keeps parents lying awake at night, glued to news stories about danger lurking around every corner. But here’s something surprising: when you look at the data, you see that most harm to children doesn’t actually come from strangers. It comes from people they already know.
The real risks aren’t flashy or dramatic. They’re quiet, often hiding in plain sight, and easy to miss if you’re not looking closely.
Here’s another one that might catch you off guard: a lot of parents would never dream of having a gun in the house, but they’re perfectly comfortable with a swimming pool in the backyard. Sounds safer, right? Yet, the numbers tell a different story—pools are far more likely to cause accidental deaths, especially for young kids.
The danger isn’t always where people expect it to be.
Picture a family doing everything they can to keep their kids safe—installing locks, steering clear of certain neighborhoods, worrying about every headline. But, the genuine risks? They’re often found much closer to home, tucked away in the routines and habits that feel completely normal.
It really goes to show: what we call “conventional wisdom” is shaped by emotion, tradition, and the stories we keep telling ourselves.
Most folks don’t stop to question what they hear. But if you do? You’ll often find that the real truth is a whole lot more complicated—and, honestly, way more useful—than the easy answer.
